video_title: Why The Nepal Flood Was WAY Scarier Than You Think
transcript: On the morning of the 26th of August 2026, some of the most terrifying footage of a natural disaster that the internet has ever seen began emerging from the Himalayas. At the main border crossing between Nepal and Tibet, a surveillance camera captured what at first appeared to be an enormous black cloud emerging from a bend in the valley. But within seconds, the cloud transformed into an almost biblical looking towering wall of water, mud, ice, and rocks that slammed directly into the border crossing that simply erased almost everything in front of it. Buildings several stories tall were torn apart and swept away. Bridges seemingly disappeared within seconds. Cars, trucks, and people were all carried downstream alongside massive boulders that weigh many tons. While videos taken further downstream showed entire rivers transform into violent torrents of mud powerful enough to push gigantic rocks around as if they were nothing but little pebbles. Thousands of years from now, our ancestors might wonder how these boulders managed to get where they ended up because of this flood. As the epic forces at work on geological time scales suddenly transpired over only a handful of minutes. And as horrifying as all of these videos were, the true scale of the catastrophe that they captured only became apparent in the days that followed. As of the time of this video's production, more than 1,300 people have been confirmed to have lost their lives across Nepal from the disaster, while more than 5,000 other people still remain missing, including around 600 foreign nationals who have been visiting the country. And on the opposite side of the border in Tibet, at least another 16 people have also been confirmed to have lost their lives, while more than 540 others also still remain missing. It therefore remains possible that the final death toll from this apocalyptic disaster could eventually approach around 7,000 people once the thousands who remain missing are fully accounted for which would almost certainly make this the deadliest flood ever recorded in all of Nepal's history. And the physical destruction left behind is almost equally difficult to comprehend as well. Nepal's government currently estimates that the flood likely inflicted around $5 billion worth of damage. An amount that's roughly equivalent to about onetenth of the entire country's annual GDP. And all in a country that is still struggling to pay off the enormous costs from the catastrophic earthquake that rocked the country only 11 years previously in 2015. But perhaps the most terrifying part of this entire disaster is the incredibly sudden and unexpected way that it all began. It wasn't caused by a rainstorm, nor by an earthquake that preceded it that could have given people an early warning. In fact, the weather high up in the mountains where the disaster began that morning was relatively clear with bright blue skies. Instead, the entire catastrophe that would go on to probably kill thousands of people, destroy billions of dollars worth of infrastructure, and send a flood pulse traveling more than 100 km downstream a river. All started at precisely 8:37 a.m. in the morning with one enormous chunk of a mountain that suddenly broke apart. This is Lang Tang Lurang, a 7,227 meter high mountain in the Himalayas just south of the border between Nepal and Tibet and the 99th highest mountain on the planet. High up along its remote northern face at an elevation of roughly 5,200 m above sea level, an enormous mass of bedrock sat beneath and supported a huge amount of glacial ice. Together, the rock and ice formed a mass hundreds of millions of tons in weight, probably equivalent to roughly 10 entire New York City blocks worth of material perched high up on the side of the mountain. For untold millennia, this mass sat here static and undisturbed. But at exactly 8:37 a.m. on the morning of the 26th of August this year, for reasons that environmental scientists are still attempting to fully understand, this massive bedrock suddenly failed all at once. The collapse took the enormous mass of glacial ice sitting above it down along with it, which immediately generated a colossal rock ice avalanche that began freef falling down more than 2,000 vertical meters of the mountainside straight towards the Lehendi River down below. The amount of potential energy stored inside of hundreds of millions of tons of rock and ice falling thousands of meters was almost unimaginable. By the time the mass crashed into the bottom of the river valley down below, scientists have estimated that the energy released by the collapse could have approached that of the atomic bomb that was dropped on Hiroshima. The impact was so incredibly violent that it generated seismic waves equivalent to a magnitude 5.2 tremor that were detected by seismic instruments all around the world. Initially, the US Geological Survey believed that an earthquake had just struck the Himalayas. But after analyzing the unusual seismic signature more closely, scientists realized that it was actually the other way around. There hadn't been any earthquake that caused the mountain to collapse. The mountain collapsing on its own had been powerful enough to create something that looked like an earthquake. And when all of that material slammed into the valley floor, the disaster transformed into something even worse. All of the tremendous friction and violence of the descent pulverized much of the falling ice almost immediately into slush and liquid water and mixed it together with the rock, sediment, dirt, and other water that was already present within the valley. Early explanations of the disaster suggested that all of this material might have hit the river and then created a temporary natural dam before the water steadily accumulated behind it and eventually explosively burst through. But a few weeks after the disaster, by this point, the emerging scientific consensus is that any natural damning effect on the river was probably pretty limited and that the catastrophic flow of the landslide itself was largely continuous from the moment the avalanche reached the valley. When the avalanche slammed into the Lehendi River, the enormous mass crashed against the opposite wall of the narrow valley and almost immediately turned westward, forcing the river ahead of it while simultaneously absorbing even more water, sediment, and rock into itself. Some preliminary analyses have suggested that this initial runup of water and debris against the opposite side of the valley may have climbed up as much as 1,500 ft or 450 m above the river channel, nearly as high as the Empire State Building. Although that doesn't mean that a literal 450 m tall wall of water thundered downstream. What did travel downstream, however, was still almost unimaginably destructive. A rapidly accelerating slurry of water, mud, ice, and rock confined within one of the steepest and narrowest river valleys that can be found anywhere in the world. The Himalayas, as you probably expect, contain the greatest vertical relief found anywhere on the Earth. And from the point where the collapse began, gravity began doing almost all of the work. As the flow raced downhill, it rapidly eroded the river banks and ripped away additional rocks and mud into itself, growing larger and larger as it went, while the narrow valley prevented most of its energy from spreading outward. Chinese scientists have since estimated that this initial debris flow reached speeds of roughly 50 m/ second, or around 110 mph. At that speed, the wall of debris could travel the length of an entire American football field from end to end in less than two seconds. And directly in its path, only around 20 km further downstream, was one of the busiest border crossings between the countries of Nepal and China. At 8:44 a.m. in the morning, only around 7 minutes after the mountain further upstream began collapsing, the flood arrived at the Kirong port and Rosu Wagatti on the Nepal Tibet border. This was the moment captured by the CCTV footage that would soon spread all around the world. And tragically, the border crossing happened to be unusually crowded that morning. Kiong and Rasuagatti form one of only two major overland trading corridors between the mountainous border of Nepal and China. But the crossing is also heavily utilized by tourists and pilgrims traveling north towards nearby Mount Kaash in Tibet. A mountain that is considered sacred to Hindus, Buddhists, and James alike. The crossing had opened at 8:00 that morning and by around 8:20 there were already an estimated 300 to 400 people who were already there waiting in the area to leave Nepal for Tibet while several dozen others were simultaneously arriving from China attempting to cross in the other direction over into Nepal. Nepal's electronic immigration system at the crossing recorded its final transaction at 8:35 a.m. that morning, just 2 minutes before the mountain collapsed and less than 10 minutes before the arrival of the flood. 89 Nepal and foreign nationals had already cleared through immigration to leave Nepal that morning, including citizens of India, China, the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and Italy. And after clearing immigration, it usually took another 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepali immigration building down towards the bridge that actually crossed the river. That essentially means that when the mountain first collapsed at 8:37 a.m. that morning, many of the people who had just cleared through immigration here were almost certainly walking directly into the path of what was coming towards them without having any idea that it even existed at all. There simply wasn't enough time for a warning. 7 minutes is barely enough time to even understand what's happening during an emergency, much less identify the source of it, communicate it across an international border and issue an evacuation order and move hundreds of people out of a deep Himalayan gorge. When that dark towering wall finally appeared around the bend in that valley, the hundreds of people down there literally only had seconds to react to it. Some immediately, desperately began trying to run uphill against a flood that was traveling faster than 100 mph. Others were simply overwhelmed. The torrent smashed into the Chinese and Nepali border facilities, completely annihilating the main port connecting the two countries together, destroying the customs and immigration buildings completely down to their very foundations and scouring much of the developed valley floor almost entirely clean. Satellite photographs taken before and after the disaster show just about everything that humanity ever built here. Buildings, roads, and infrastructure all just completely gone without a trace hardly remaining afterwards. As if nothing had ever even existed there at all in the first place. And Kong was only the beginning of this disaster. Almost immediately after crossing into Nepal, the flood tore into a border town called Tamir, a town that had rapidly expanded over the previous decade because of the growth in trade with China. The dry port in Tamir where trans Himalayan cargo was staged at was completely destroyed along with much of the nearby 111 megawatt Rasuagatti hydroelect electric project that had only just opened its operations 2 years previously in 2024. After nearly a decade of construction, hundreds of local residents and workers disappeared here as the torrent continued racing downstream. And only minutes later, at roughly 8:50 a.m., it reached Sir BC, a regional market and tourist hub positioned where the Lang Train River joins the larger river system. Here, the flow carved away portions of the mountain side itself and devastated settlements that were on both sides of the river, destroying the older town on the eastern bank and much of the newer main street on the western side that had been lined with businesses and hotels. At 8:50 a.m., only around 13 minutes after the initial collapse had begun, the hydraological monitoring station here at Sir Rubisi stopped transmitting data entirely. Its last measurement taken 10 minutes earlier at 8:40 a.m. had shown the river at only 1.62 m deep, which was perfectly normal. By around 9:00 a.m., Nepal's flood forecasting division was finally receiving reports that an enormous flood had entered into the river system from the direction of Tibet. But it was only at 9:15 and 9:16 a.m., nearly 40 minutes after the original mountain collapse, were emergency SMS warnings finally sent out to the nearly 680,000 people living along riverbank areas further downstream in the country. By then, the communities that were closest to the source of the collapse had already effectively ceased to exist and hadn't received any warning before their doom had arrived. Further downstream though, those warnings became increasingly important because the floods still had a huge amount of elevation left to descend through. The torrent continued through the towns of Milong, Bertraati Bazaar, and Trashuli Bazaar, ripping apart bridges, roads, power lines, villages, and additional hydroelectric facilities as it went. 19 bridges and roughly 40 km of highways were damaged or destroyed, while massive boulders carried along by the current were filmed by onlookers tumbling through the river as if they were nothing but toys. Further downstream at the town of Gauchi, more than 100 km away from the origin of the collapse, the river still reportedly rose by as much as 9 m and only 30 minutes after the surge arrived. By the time the flood had reached this far, the material inside of it had descended more than 4500 vertical meters from the Himalayan mountains where it had all begun at. And it still wasn't finished either. Bodies of victims were recovered from the river almost all the way down towards the plains near Nepal's border with India. While a flood pulse roughly one meter high was still detectable all the way down here in the border region too several hundred kilometers downstream of where the mountain had first collapsed. In other words, something that began with a single section of rock and ice breaking loose from one remote Himalayan mountainside had managed to physically alter an entire river system across a substantial portion of a whole country. The human consequences are obviously the worst part of this disaster. But the economic consequences for Nepal will also linger around for years and perhaps even decades to come. Nepal was already one of the poorest countries in Asia. And it had already spent most of the 21st century repeatedly attempting to recover from one crisis after another. For a decade between 1996 and 2006, the country was wrecked by a brutal civil war that pitted a mauist insurgency against the government that killed more than 17,000 people. Then less than a decade later in 2015, Nepal was devastated by a magnitude 7.8 earthquake that killed thousands more and inflicted around $9 billion worth of economic damage. Government borrowing nearly doubled as a share of the economy since then. just in order to recover. Nepal is an extremely mountainous country filled with big rivers that descend rapidly down from the Himalayas which gives it one of the greatest untapped concentrations of hydroelectric potential anywhere in Asia. In theory as much as 43 gawatt of Nepalese hydro power could eventually be commercially exploited enough to supply Nepal itself while exporting huge excesses of electricity south into increasingly energy hungry India. Developing this hydropower potential has therefore become one of Nepal's biggest strategies for reducing its presently large economic dependence on remittances from the hundreds of thousands of Nepales who leave the country every year to work abroad. But unfortunately, many of the best locations to construct hydroelectric infrastructure in Nepal are along precisely the same steep Himalayan river valleys that are most exposed to disasters like this one. The August flood destroyed or damaged 14 hydroelectric projects and knocked out around 12% of Nepal's total generating capacity. So Nepal now faces the extraordinarily cruel situation where some of the infrastructure that it was building to make its economy more resilient in the future has itself become one of the greatest sources of loss from this disaster. All of that is completely destroyed now, which will no doubt hinder Nepal's ability to continue trading with China, which will further reduce the country's ability to be able to adequately recover. And the Nepali tourism industry, another one of the country's most important sources of foreign currency could suffer as well, especially since the crippled corridor at Rasu Wagatti was heavily used by international tourists and Hindu and Buddhist pilgrims traveling towards Mount Kaos.
